title: Behavioural Adaptations
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Behavioural Adaptations Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Examine how particular structural features and behaviours of living things enable their survival in specific habitats (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on behavioural adaptations: why bilbies come out at night, whales migrate, possums hibernate and magpies swoop. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: A behavioural adaptation is something a living thing does.
body_html:
How to think about it

A behavioural adaptation is an action that helps a living thing survive.

  • Ask what the problem is: heat, cold, little food, predators or finding a mate.
  • Then link the behaviour: hiding in a burrow by day, migrating to warm water, hibernating, living in a mob, showing a frill.
  • Body parts (claws, ears, spines) are structural adaptations. They often work together with behaviours.
Example

A kangaroo licks its forearms on a hot day. Why?

the saliva evaporates

evaporation takes away heat

Answer: to cool down

Example

Humpback whales swim north in winter. Why?

the water further north is warmer

the calves are born there

Answer: to give birth in warm water

Common mistakes

  • Calling a body part a behaviour (claws are structural; digging is the behaviour).
  • Forgetting that Australian seasons are opposite to the northern hemisphere (winter is June to August).
  • Thinking animals change their bodies because they want to.

faq.q: What is the difference between nocturnal and diurnal?
faq.a: Nocturnal animals, such as bilbies and possums, are active at night. Diurnal animals, such as kookaburras and emus, are active during the day.
Yes. Some plants turn their leaves towards the light or close their flowers at night. These are responses to their surroundings.
They feed in cold Antarctic waters in summer, then swim north along the Australian coast in winter to give birth in warmer water.

items.q: Is webbed feet a structural feature or a behaviour?
items.e: Structural adaptations are body parts; behavioural adaptations are things an animal does.

items.q: A plant's leaves turn to face the sun. How does this help?
c: The leaves get more light to make food.
items.e: Plants use light to make their food.

items.q: A magpie swoops at people near its nest in spring. Why does it do this?
c: to protect its eggs and chicks
to stay cool and save water
to stay safe from daytime predators
items.e: This is a behavioural adaptation: something the magpie does that helps it survive.

items.q: A flying fox fans and licks its wings on hot days. Why does it do this?

to escape the heat of the plains
items.e: This is a behavioural adaptation: something the flying fox does that helps it survive.

items.q: A possum sleeps in a tree hollow during the day and feeds at night. Why does it do this?

items.q: Is a waxy coating on its leaves a structural feature or a behaviour?

items.q: How does a frill-necked lizard scare away a predator?

items.q: Why do many desert animals rest in burrows during the day?

items.q: Why do kangaroos live in mobs?

items.e: Group living is a behavioural adaptation.

items.q: A short-tailed shearwater flies across the Pacific Ocean each year. Why does it do this?

items.q: Is long back legs for hopping a structural feature or a behaviour?

items.q: Why do some animals migrate?

items.q: What does it mean when an animal hibernates?
c: It moves to a new country.

items.e: Its heart rate and body temperature drop.

items.q: A platypus closes its eyes and ears when it dives. Why does it do this?
